behavior.overview: This repository is a full-stack e-commerce monolith consisting of a Django-based REST API backend and a React-based frontend application. The system supports typical e-commerce functionality, including product management, user authentication, profile management, order processing, payments, reviews, and shipping addresses.

partitions.name: Backend Services (ecommerce/)
partitions.role: The core business logic, database models, and API endpoints for the e-commerce system.
partitions.functionality: Handles data persistence and business rules for entities like users, products, orders, payments, and reviews, exposing these via Django-based REST serializers and views.

partitions.name: Frontend Application (frontend/)
partitions.role: The client-side React application that provides the user interface.
partitions.functionality: Implements the presentation layer using React, Redux for state management, and Axios to communicate with the Django backend. It includes screens for user authentication, product browsing, cart management, and order checkout.

partitions.name: Configuration and Deployment
partitions.functionality: Contains server configuration (WSGI/ASGI), Django project settings for various environments (local, production), and Docker configuration files.

partitions.name: Static Assets
partitions.functionality: Houses product images, media uploads, and static assets such as CSS, JavaScript bundles for the admin interface, and the frontend web manifest.

context_record.business_goal: Modernize the existing e-commerce monolith for improved scalability and maintainability while allowing incremental evolution.
context_record.problem_statement: The existing monolithic architecture suffers from scalability and maintainability issues, particularly under peak traffic loads.

blueprint.selected_pattern: Strangler Fig – Incremental Service Extraction with Event-Driven Architecture
blueprint.rationale: The Strangler Fig pattern enables incremental extraction of bounded contexts from the existing Django monolith into independently deployable services while preserving existing functionality. Combining synchronous REST for user‑facing interactions with asynchronous event‑driven communication between services satisfies the need for higher scalability and fault isolation without a big‑bang rewrite. Managed AWS services (API Gateway, Fargate, RDS, SQS) provide operational benefits and align with the cloud preference.
blueprint.stakeholder_view: Customers and administrators interact with a responsive React web UI. The UI calls the API Gateway, which routes requests to the appropriate backend service (Product, User, Order, Payment, Review). The system must handle traffic spikes, stay highly available, and allow new features to be added without downtime. Administrators gain the ability to evolve each domain independently, improving maintainability and time‑to‑market.
blueprint.technical_view: The architecture consists of an AWS API Gateway front‑end, a React SPA, five domain services (Product, User, Order, Payment, Review) each running as containerised Django applications on AWS Fargate, an Amazon SQS event bus for asynchronous inter‑service communication, and a shared Amazon RDS PostgreSQL instance (or per‑service schemas). The API Gateway also forwards legacy monolith traffic during migration. All services expose REST endpoints for UI calls and publish/consume domain events via SQS to achieve decoupling and scalability.
constraints_addressed: Cloud: AWS managed services used where they add clear operational or scalability benefit.
Budget: Incremental migration avoids large upfront cost; services are containerised on Fargate with pay‑as‑you‑go pricing.
Scalability: Auto‑scaling groups for each service and event‑driven decoupling handle peak traffic.
Compliance: No new technology stacks introduced; existing Django security model retained.
Migration: Brownfield Strangler Fig approach with defined migration steps.
assumptions: The existing Django codebase can be refactored into separate Django projects per domain.
Data can be migrated to separate schemas in the same RDS instance without downtime.
Team has capability to operate containerised services on AWS Fargate.
open_risks: Data consistency during the period when both monolith and extracted services access the same tables.
Operational overhead of managing multiple services and the event bus.
Potential cost increase from managed services if traffic spikes are sustained.

migration_steps.title: Introduce API Gateway and routing layer
migration_steps.objective: Create a unified entry point that can route traffic to the existing monolith and future services.
changes: Configure routes to forward all current API paths to the monolith.
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: All requests continue to hit the monolith; API Gateway acts as a transparent proxy.
migration_steps.exit_condition: API Gateway is live and routing correctly.

migration_steps.title: Extract Product Service
migration_steps.objective: Move product management functionality into an independent service.
changes: Create a new Django project for product domain.
Migrate product models, serializers, and views.
Update API Gateway route /products to point to the new service.
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Initial data sync from monolith to new service database; read‑through fallback to monolith during cut‑over.
migration_steps.exit_condition: Product API responses are served by Product Service with no functional regression.

migration_steps.title: Extract User Service (authentication, profile, shipping)
changes: Create a new Django project for user domain.
Migrate authentication, profile, and address logic.
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Shared user tables initially; later migrate to service‑specific schema.
migration_steps.exit_condition: User‑related endpoints are served by User Service and JWT issuance works.

migration_steps.title: Introduce Event Bus and extract Order Service
migration_steps.objective: Decouple order processing and enable asynchronous workflows.
changes: Deploy Amazon SQS queues for OrderCreated and PaymentProcessed events.
Create Order Service handling order lifecycle and publishing events.
Modify Order Service to consume payment events.
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Order data initially duplicated; eventual single source of truth in Order Service.
migration_steps.exit_condition: Orders can be placed via API Gateway and processed through the event bus without errors.

migration_steps.title: Extract Payment and Review Services, then decommission monolith
migration_steps.objective: Complete domain extraction and retire the legacy monolith.
changes: Create Payment Service and Review Service with their own queues.
Update API Gateway routes for /payments and /reviews.
Gradually disable monolith endpoints once all domains are verified.
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: All domains now independent; data resides in per‑service schemas.
migration_steps.exit_condition: All functional tests pass against the new services and the monolith is no longer receiving traffic.

adrs.title: ADR-001: Service Decomposition using Domain‑Driven Design
adrs.context: The monolith mixes unrelated business capabilities, causing scalability and maintainability problems.
adrs.decision: Define bounded contexts (Product, User, Order, Payment, Review, Shipping) and extract each into its own Django service.
adrs.rationale: DDD aligns service boundaries with business capabilities, reducing coupling and enabling independent scaling (KB‑E001, KB‑E002).
alternatives_considered: Keep a single monolith and scale vertically.
positive_consequences: Independent deployment and scaling per domain.

adrs.title: ADR-002: Data Ownership and Persistence Strategy
adrs.context: Shared database tables across domains hinder independent scaling and fault isolation.
adrs.decision: Give each service ownership of its own schema (or tables) within a shared Amazon RDS PostgreSQL instance, migrating data during extraction steps.
adrs.rationale: Separate data ownership reduces cross‑service coupling and aligns with DDD principles (KB‑E002, KB‑E004).
alternatives_considered: Continue using a single shared schema.
positive_consequences: Easier to scale storage per service.

adrs.title: ADR-003: Integration Style – Hybrid Synchronous/Asynchronous
adrs.context: User‑facing operations require low latency, while internal processes can tolerate eventual consistency.
adrs.decision: Expose REST endpoints via API Gateway for UI calls (synchronous) and use Amazon SQS for inter‑service events (asynchronous).
adrs.rationale: Hybrid approach provides responsive UI while leveraging event‑driven decoupling for scalability and fault tolerance (KB‑E002, KB‑E005).
alternatives_considered: Purely synchronous REST calls between services.
Fully event‑driven architecture without any REST.

adrs.title: ADR-004: Scaling and Availability Strategy
adrs.context: Peak traffic spikes cause degradation in the monolith.
adrs.decision: Run each service as a container on AWS Fargate with auto‑scaling, fronted by API Gateway, and use RDS Multi‑AZ for database high availability.
adrs.rationale: Container‑based deployment and managed services enable automatic scaling and resilience without managing servers (KB‑E002, KB‑E006).
alternatives_considered: Scale the monolith vertically on larger EC2 instances.
negative_consequences: Potential increase in AWS spend if not monitored.

adrs.title: ADR-005: Brownfield Migration – Strangler Fig Strategy
adrs.context: The existing system must stay operational while new services are introduced.
adrs.decision: Adopt a Strangler Fig approach: route traffic through API Gateway, incrementally replace monolith endpoints with extracted services, and finally retire the monolith.
adrs.rationale: Allows continuous delivery, minimizes downtime, and leverages existing code during transition (KB‑E002, KB‑E004).
alternatives_considered: Parallel run of monolith and new system with manual cut‑over.
negative_consequences: Need to maintain two codebases temporarily.

adrs.title: ADR-006: Technology Conservation vs Replacement
adrs.context: The repository already uses Django (Python) for backend and React for frontend.
adrs.decision: Retain Django and React as the primary development frameworks; introduce only AWS managed services (API Gateway, Fargate, RDS, SQS) where they provide clear operational benefit.
adrs.rationale: Preserves existing developer expertise and code investment; avoids unnecessary rewrites while still achieving scalability through managed infrastructure.
alternatives_considered: Rewrite services in a different language/framework (e.g., Go, Node.js).
Adopt a serverless approach with AWS Lambda.
negative_consequences: May miss out on language‑specific performance gains.

retrieved_knowledge.content:
The reviewed studies reveal several distinct approaches to monolith decomposition, each with specific advantages for e-commerce contexts.

**a. Domain-Driven Design (DDD) Approaches:** Multiple studies emphasize Domain-Driven Design as a foundational approach for identifying service boundaries in e-commerce systems. Abgaz et al. [1] identify DDD as a critical component of their Monolith to Microservices Decomposition Framework (M2MDF), noting its effectiveness in creating business-aligned service boundaries. Kaloudis [6] reinforces this approach, demonstrating how DDD enables better service cohesion and reduced coupling. In e-commerce contexts, natural domain boundaries often align with business capabilities, such as customer management, product catalog, order processing, payment handling, and inventory management.

Microservices architecture has emerged as a compelling alternative, offering the promise of enhanced scalability, improved fault tolerance, and greater development agility [1]. By decomposing monolithic applications into smaller, independently deployable services, organizations can achieve better resource utilization, faster deployment cycles, and improved system resilience.

Event-driven architecture (EDA) patterns have gained particular attention in the context of microservices migration, especially for e-commerce systems where business processes are inherently event-oriented. Customer actions such as placing orders, updating profiles, or processing payments naturally translate to domain events that can drive system behavior [5]. The asynchronous nature of event-driven communication provides better decoupling between services, enhanced fault tolerance, and improved scalability compared to synchronous request-response patterns [4].

## 2.2 Monolithic and Microservices Architectures Comparison *(printed p. 478)*

In the e-commerce landscape, choosing between microservices and traditional monolithic architectures requires careful consideration of various factors. Monolithic architectures, characterized by their single, tightly coupled codebase. However, when e-commerce systems increase in size, they frequently face scalability and maintenance issues. Microservices provide an alternative approach by decomposing monolithic applications into smaller, self-contained services [6]. This decomposition results in fine-grained services, each focusing on a specific business capability. Scalability is one of the most major advantages of microservices. E-commerce platforms often experience fluctuating traffic patterns, especially during promotions or seasonal events. Microservices enable organisations to scale individual services, ensuring that resources are deployed efficiently to manage workload properly.

## Introduction — relevante Absätze zur E-Commerce-Migration *(printed p. 2)*

The rapid evolution of e-commerce platforms has necessitated architectural paradigm shifts to meet increasing demands for scalability, reliability, and agility [2]. Traditional monolithic architectures, while providing simplicity in development and deployment, often become bottlenecks as e-commerce systems scale to handle millions of transactions and users [3]. The centralized nature of monolithic systems creates inherent limitations in terms of independent scaling, technology diversity, and fault isolation, making them unsuitable for modern e-commerce requirements.

features.name: Product Management
features.description: Enable administrators to create, update, and delete product listings via the backend API.
features.scenario: An administrator uses the admin UI to add a new product, modifies its price, and then removes an obsolete product. Each action is performed through the REST API.
acceptance_criteria: The new product appears in the product catalog after creation.
Updates to the product are reflected in subsequent GET requests.
Deleted products are no longer returned by the API.
Each API call returns the appropriate HTTP status code (201 for create, 200 for update, 204 for delete).

features.name: User Authentication
features.description: Provide secure login and token issuance for customers.
features.scenario: A customer enters a valid email and password on the login page and receives a JWT token that is used for subsequent protected API calls.
acceptance_criteria: Valid credentials result in a JWT token returned in the response.
Invalid credentials return a 401 Unauthorized response.
The issued token can be used to access an endpoint that requires authentication.
Tokens expire according to the configured policy and are rejected after expiration.

features.name: Profile Management
features.description: Allow authenticated users to view and edit their personal profile information.
features.scenario: A logged‑in user updates their phone number and mailing address through the profile page, then retrieves the profile to verify the changes.
acceptance_criteria: Profile updates are persisted and returned correctly on a subsequent GET request.
Invalid data (e.g., malformed email) results in a validation error response.
Only the owner of the profile can modify their data; attempts by other users are rejected.

features.name: Order Processing
features.description: Create and manage customer orders, including inventory reservation and confirmation.
features.scenario: A customer adds items to the cart and submits an order. The system creates an order record, reserves inventory, and sends an order confirmation email.
acceptance_criteria: An order record is created with correct line items and total amount.
Inventory quantities are decremented accordingly.
An order confirmation email is dispatched to the customer's email address.
If inventory is insufficient, the order is rejected with an appropriate error message.

features.name: Payments Integration
features.description: Process customer payments securely through a third‑party payment gateway.
features.scenario: During checkout, the customer provides payment details, the system forwards them to the payment provider, and records the transaction outcome.
acceptance_criteria: Successful payment results in the order status being set to "Paid".
Failed payment returns a clear error to the user and leaves the order in a pending state.
No duplicate charges are created for the same order.
Payment data is never stored in the system beyond the transaction token.

features.name: Reviews Management
features.description: Enable customers to submit and view product reviews with moderation workflow.
features.scenario: An authenticated customer writes a 5‑star review with text for a purchased product. The review is stored as pending and becomes visible after moderator approval.
acceptance_criteria: The review is saved with the correct rating and text.
The review is not displayed publicly until its status changes to approved.
Moderators can change the review status to approved or rejected.
Aggregated product rating reflects only approved reviews.

features.name: Shipping Addresses Management
features.description: Allow users to add, edit, and delete shipping addresses in their account.
features.scenario: A user adds a new shipping address, updates the street name of an existing address, and deletes an outdated address, then proceeds to checkout using the default address.
acceptance_criteria: New addresses appear in the user's address list after creation.
Edits are reflected in subsequent retrievals of the address list.
Deleted addresses are no longer present in the list.
The default address is automatically selected during checkout.

features.name: Scalable Performance Under Peak Load
features.description: Ensure the system can handle substantially higher peak traffic without degradation.
features.scenario: During a simulated traffic surge that exceeds typical peak load, the application continues to serve requests without a noticeable increase in error rates or response time.
acceptance_criteria: Error rate remains low (no spike in 5xx responses) during the surge.
Response times stay within the range experienced under normal load, with no user‑perceived slowdown.
System resources scale (e.g., additional containers or instances) to accommodate the load.

features.name: High Availability
features.description: Maintain service availability during peak periods and component failures.
features.scenario: When a primary application instance becomes unavailable, traffic is automatically rerouted to healthy instances, and users experience no interruption.
acceptance_criteria: Service remains reachable throughout the failure event.
Failover occurs without requiring manual intervention.
Ongoing user sessions are preserved or gracefully re‑established.

features.name: Responsive Customer‑Facing Interactions
features.description: Keep all customer‑facing UI actions responsive even under load.
features.scenario: A customer browses product listings, adds items to the cart, and proceeds to checkout, observing smooth UI behavior without hanging or long waits.
acceptance_criteria: Page loads and UI updates occur without noticeable lag.
No UI elements become unresponsive during typical user flows.
User feedback (e.g., loading indicators) appears promptly when backend processing is in progress.
